subject: math
title: Grade 4 Equations and Inequalities
seo_title: Grade 4 Equations and Inequalities Worksheets: Free Math with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Solve equations that involve whole numbers up to 50 in various contexts, and verify solutions
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on equations and inequalities for the Ontario curriculum: letters as unknowns, pan balances, solving n + 8 = 23 and 4 × n = 36, checking solutions, and inequalities like n + 5 < 12 graphed on a number line. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Use the inverse to find the unknown: n + 8 = 23, so n = 23 − 8 = 15.
key_sub: Check by putting the answer back in: 15 + 8 = 23. For n + 5 < 12, the solutions are the whole numbers less than 7, so 7 gets no dot.
body_html:
Letters stand for unknown numbers

An equation has an = sign. Both sides have the same value, like a pan balance that is level. A letter such as n stands for a number we do not know yet. n is a variable.

Solve with the inverse

To solve an equation, find the number that makes both sides equal. Use the inverse operation to undo what was done to n.

EquationUndo itSolution
n + 8 = 2323 − 8n = 15
n − 9 = 2727 + 9n = 36
4 × n = 3636 ÷ 4n = 9
n ÷ 4 = 66 × 4n = 24
Example 1

Solve n + 8 = 23.

Subtraction undoes addition: n = 23 − 8 = 15.

Answer: n = 15

Check your solution

Put your answer back in place of the letter. If both sides are equal, the answer is right.

Example 2

Is n = 15 the solution of n + 8 = 23?

15 + 8 = 23. Both sides are 23.

Answer: Yes

Inequalities

An inequality uses < (is less than) or > (is greater than). It has many solutions, not just one. Solve it like an equation first, then decide which side the solutions are on. On a number line, put a dot on every whole-number solution.

Example 3

Solve n + 5 < 12 and graph the solutions.

Think of n + 5 = 12: n = 7. But 7 + 5 = 12 is not less than 12. Try 6: 6 + 5 = 11, and 11 < 12 is true. So n < 7: the whole numbers 0 to 6.

Answer: n < 7

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
n + 8 = 23, so n = 31 (23 + 8)Use the inverse: 23 − 8 = 15
n − 9 = 27, so n = 18 (27 − 9)Undo − 9 by adding: 27 + 9 = 36
4 × n = 36, so n = 32 (36 − 4)Undo × 4 by dividing: 36 ÷ 4 = 9
n < 7, so put a dot on 77 is not less than 7. The dots stop at 6
n > 7, so put dots on 0 to 6> means greater: dots on 8 and greater
The letter n means 14n is just a name for the unknown number

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about equations and inequalities in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario Grade 4 Algebra strand (C2), students use letters as variables, solve equations with whole numbers up to 50, and check their solutions. They also solve inequalities with addition and subtraction up to 20, like n + 5 < 12, and graph the solutions on a number line.

faq.q: How do you solve an equation like n + 8 = 23 or 4 × n = 36?
faq.a: Use the inverse operation. Subtraction undoes addition, so n = 23 − 8 = 15. Division undoes multiplication, so n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Then put the answer back in to check it.

faq.q: How do you solve and graph an inequality in Grade 4?
faq.a: Solve it like an equation, then test a number to see which side the solutions are on. For n + 5 < 12, n = 7 would make 12, so the solutions are the whole numbers less than 7: put dots on 0 to 6, with no dot on 7.

faq.q: Why do Grade 4 students use letters like n in math?
faq.a: A letter is a variable: it stands for a number we do not know yet. Using letters prepares students for algebra in later grades. Any letter works, so 3 × n = 24 and 3 × k = 24 both have the solution 8.

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?
items.e: The pans balance, so both sides have the same value: n + 6 = 14. The letter n stands for the unknown number. (n = 8, because 8 + 6 = 14.)

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?
items.e: There are 3 blocks, and each block is n. 3 blocks are 3 × n, so 3 × n = 15. Not n + 3: the 3 tells how many blocks, not a mass of 3. (n = 5.)

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?
items.e: The left pan has 20 and the right pan has k + 12, so 20 = k + 12. The = sign can have the unknown on either side. (k = 8.)

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?
items.e: The left pan has y − 5 and the right pan has 9, so y − 5 = 9. 5 − y starts with 5, not with y. (y = 14.)

items.q: The pans balance. What is n?
items.e: n + 9 = 17. Use the inverse: n = 17 − 9 = 8. Check: 8 + 9 = 17. Not 26: that adds 9 instead of taking it away.

items.q: The pans balance. What is n?
items.e: 4 equal blocks balance 20, so 4 × n = 20. Share 20 into 4 equal parts: n = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Check: 4 × 5 = 20. Not 16: that subtracts 4. Not 24: that adds 4. Not 80: that multiplies.

items.q: The pans balance. What is m?
items.e: m + 18 = 25, so m = 25 − 18 = 7. Check: 7 + 18 = 25. Not 43: that adds. Not 13: that takes the smaller digit from the larger (8 − 5 instead of 15 − 8).

items.q: The pans balance. What is p?
items.e: p − 7 = 12. Undo − 7 by adding 7: p = 12 + 7 = 19. Check: 19 − 7 = 12. Not 5: that subtracts 7 again instead of adding.

items.q: In 7 + n = 15, what does the letter n stand for?
items.e: A letter in an equation stands for an unknown number. Here n = 8, because 7 + 8 = 15. It is not 14 (n is the 14th letter of the alphabet), and it is not just any number: only 8 works.

items.q: Which equation means “a number plus 9 is 21”?
items.e: Let n be the number. “a number plus 9 is 21” is n + 9 = 21. Then n = 12.

items.q: Which equation means “6 times a number is 42”?
items.e: Let n be the number. “6 times a number is 42” is 6 × n = 42. Then n = 7.

items.q: Which equation means “a number take away 8 is 30”?
items.e: Let n be the number. “a number take away 8 is 30” is n − 8 = 30. Then n = 38. 8 − n starts with 8, not with the number.

items.q: Which equation means “a number divided by 5 is 7”?
items.e: Let n be the number. “a number divided by 5 is 7” is n ÷ 5 = 7. Then n = 35. 5 ÷ n divides 5, not the number.
You can add in any order: 13 + 6 = 6 + 13. So m = 13. Not 19: that is the value of the right side, 6 + 13. Not 7: that is 13 − 6.

items.q: Which equation is true when n = 7?
items.e: Put 7 in place of n. 7 + 8 = 15, so n + 8 = 15 is true.

items.q: Which equation is true when y = 6?
items.e: Put 6 in place of y. 5 × 6 = 30, so 5 × y = 30 is true.

items.q: What is the value of k + 9 when k = 4?
items.e: Put 4 in place of k: 4 + 9 = 13. Not 5: that subtracts. Not 36: that multiplies.

items.q: What is the value of 7 × n when n = 6?
items.e: 7 × n means 7 times n. Put 6 in place of n: 7 × 6 = 42. Not 76: the 7 and the 6 are not written side by side. Not 13: that adds. Not 1: that subtracts.

items.q: The pans balance. What is a?
items.e: The right side is 30 + 5 = 35. So a + 10 = 35, and a = 35 − 10 = 25. Not 35: that is the value of the right side. Not 20: that forgets the 5. Not 45: that adds 10.

items.q: Zoe writes 3 × n = 24. Lucas writes 3 × k = 24. What is true?
items.e: Any letter can stand for the unknown. In both equations 3 × 8 = 24, so n and k are both 8. The letter is just a name. It does not change the number. Not 21: that subtracts 3.

items.q: Solve: n + 8 = 23. What is n?
items.e: Subtraction undoes addition: n = 23 − 8 = 15. Check: 15 + 8 = 23. Not 31: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 25: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: 17 + n = 42. What is n?
items.e: Subtraction undoes addition: n = 42 − 17 = 25. Check: 17 + 25 = 42. Not 59: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 35: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: y + 26 = 50. What is y?
items.e: Subtraction undoes addition: y = 50 − 26 = 24. Check: 24 + 26 = 50. Not 76: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 36: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: n − 9 = 27. What is n?
items.e: n is the number you start with. Addition undoes subtraction: n = 27 + 9 = 36. Check: 36 − 9 = 27. Not 18: that subtracts instead of adding. Not 26: that forgets to carry the ten.

items.q: Solve: p − 14 = 29. What is p?
items.e: p is the number you start with. Addition undoes subtraction: p = 29 + 14 = 43. Check: 43 − 14 = 29. Not 15: that subtracts instead of adding. Not 33: that forgets to carry the ten.

items.q: Solve: 45 − n = 18. What is n?
items.e: 45 take away what leaves 18? n = 45 − 18 = 27. Check: 45 − 27 = 18. Not 63: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 33: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: 32 − t = 15. What is t?
items.e: 32 take away what leaves 15? t = 32 − 15 = 17. Check: 32 − 17 = 15. Not 47: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 23: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: 4 × n = 36. What is n?
items.e: Division undoes multiplication: n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Check: 4 × 9 = 36. Not 32: that subtracts 4. Not 40: that adds 4. Not 144: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: m × 6 = 42. What is m?
items.e: Division undoes multiplication: m = 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Check: 6 × 7 = 42. Not 36: that subtracts 6. Not 48: that adds 6. Not 252: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: 8 × b = 48. What is b?
items.e: Division undoes multiplication: b = 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Check: 8 × 6 = 48. Not 40: that subtracts 8. Not 56: that adds 8. Not 384: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: 7 × n = 28. What is n?
items.e: Division undoes multiplication: n = 28 ÷ 7 = 4. Check: 7 × 4 = 28. Not 21: that subtracts 7. Not 35: that adds 7. Not 196: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: n ÷ 4 = 6. What is n?
items.e: n is the number you start with. Multiplication undoes division: n = 6 × 4 = 24. Check: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Not 2: that subtracts. Not 10: that adds. Not 20: that is 4 × 5, one group short.

items.q: Solve: 42 ÷ n = 7. What is n?
items.e: 42 shared into how many groups gives 7 in each? 42 ÷ 7 = 6, so n = 6. Check: 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Not 35: that subtracts. Not 49: that adds. Not 294: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: w ÷ 5 = 8. What is w?
items.e: Multiplication undoes division: w = 8 × 5 = 40. Check: 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Not 3: that subtracts. Not 13: that adds. Not 45: that is one group of 5 too many.

items.q: Solve: 31 = n + 12. What is n?
items.e: The = sign can come first. n + 12 = 31, so n = 31 − 12 = 19. Check: 19 + 12 = 31. Not 43: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 21: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Solve: 50 = 5 × k. What is k?
items.e: 5 × k = 50, so k = 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Check: 5 × 10 = 50. Not 45: that subtracts. Not 55: that adds. Not 250: that multiplies.

items.q: Solve: 20 = h − 16. What is h?
items.e: h − 16 = 20. Undo − 16 by adding: h = 20 + 16 = 36. Check: 36 − 16 = 20. Not 4: that subtracts instead of adding.

items.q: What is n in the bar model?
items.e: The two parts make the whole: 19 + n = 47. So n = 47 − 19 = 28. Check: 19 + 28 = 47. Not 66: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 32: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: What is m in the bar model?
items.e: m is the whole, so add the parts: m = 16 + 25 = 41. Not 9: that subtracts. Not 31: that forgets to carry the ten from 6 + 5 = 11.

items.q: Solve: n + 15 = 20 + 18. What is n?
items.e: The right side is 20 + 18 = 38. So n + 15 = 38, and n = 38 − 15 = 23. Not 38: that is the right side. Not 53: that adds 15. Not 13: 15 is less than 20, so n is more than 18, not less.

items.q: Which equation has n = 6 as its solution?
items.e: Put 6 in place of n and work out each left side. 6 + 9 = 15, so n + 9 = 15 is true. The other equations are false when n = 6.

items.q: Which equation has n = 8 as its solution?
items.e: Put 8 in place of n and work out each left side. 4 × 8 = 32, so 4 × n = 32 is true. The other equations are false when n = 8.

items.q: Which equation has y = 12 as its solution?
items.e: Put 12 in place of y and work out each left side. 30 − 12 = 18, so 30 − y = 18 is true. The other equations are false when y = 12.

items.q: Which equation has k = 7 as its solution?
items.e: Put 7 in place of k and work out each left side. 42 ÷ 7 = 6, so 42 ÷ k = 6 is true. The other equations are false when k = 7.

items.q: Is n = 9 a solution of n + 7 = 16?
items.e: Put 9 in place of n: 9 + 7 = 16. Both sides are equal, so yes, 9 is a solution.

items.q: Is n = 7 a solution of n − 8 = 15?
items.e: 7 − 8 does not give 15, so 7 is not a solution. 7 came from 15 − 8: subtracting instead of adding. Undo − 8 by adding: n = 15 + 8 = 23. Check: 23 − 8 = 15.

items.q: Is n = 8 a solution of 5 × n = 40?
items.e: Put 8 in place of n: 5 × 8 = 40. Both sides are equal, so yes, 8 is a solution.

items.q: Is n = 2 a solution of n ÷ 3 = 6?
items.e: 2 ÷ 3 is not 6, so 2 is not a solution. Undo ÷ 3 by multiplying: n = 6 × 3 = 18. Check: 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

items.q: Is n = 18 a solution of 34 − n = 16?
items.e: Put 18 in place of n: 34 − 18 = 16. Both sides are equal, so yes, 18 is a solution.

items.q: Is n = 64 a solution of n + 19 = 45?
items.e: Put 64 in place of n: 64 + 19 is 83, not 45. So 64 is not a solution. The solution is 26. Check: 26 + 19 = 45. 64 comes from adding 19 instead of subtracting it.

items.q: Arjun solves n + 12 = 30 and gets n = 42. What did he do?
items.e: Check: 42 + 12 does not give 30, so 42 is wrong. He added. Subtraction is the inverse of addition. The answer is n = 18. Check: 18 + 12 = 30.

items.q: Sofia solves n − 6 = 14 and gets n = 8. What did she do?
items.e: Check: 8 − 6 does not give 14, so 8 is wrong. She subtracted. Addition is the inverse of subtraction. The answer is n = 20. Check: 20 − 6 = 14.

items.q: Emma solves 6 × n = 42 and gets n = 252. What did she do?
items.e: Check: 6 × 252 does not give 42, so 252 is wrong. She multiplied. Division is the inverse of multiplication. The answer is n = 7. Check: 6 × 7 = 42.

items.q: Maya solves n ÷ 4 = 5 and gets n = 20. What did she do?
items.e: Check: 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Both sides are equal, so nothing is wrong. She is right.

items.q: Mateo solves 25 − n = 9 and gets n = 34. What did he do?
items.e: Check: 25 − 34 does not give 9, so 34 is wrong. He added 25 + 9. But 25 take away n leaves 9, so subtract: 25 − 9. The answer is n = 16. Check: 25 − 16 = 9.

items.q: Benjamin solves n − 9 = 21 and gets n = 12. What did he do?
items.e: Check: 12 − 9 does not give 21, so 12 is wrong. He subtracted. Addition is the inverse of subtraction. The answer is n = 30. Check: 30 − 9 = 21.

items.q: Which can you use to check that n = 15 is the solution of n + 8 = 23?
items.e: To check, put 15 back in place of n: 15 + 8 = 23. Both sides are equal, so 15 is right. The other number sentences are true, but they do not put 15 in place of n.

items.q: Which can you use to check that n = 7 is the solution of 6 × n = 42?
items.e: To check, put 7 back in place of n: 6 × 7 = 42. Both sides are equal, so 7 is right. The other number sentences are true, but they do not put 7 in place of n.

items.q: Which can you use to check that n = 37 is the solution of n − 13 = 24?
items.e: To check, put 37 back in place of n: 37 − 13 = 24. Both sides are equal, so 37 is right. The other number sentences are true, but they do not put 37 in place of n.

items.q: Try each number in n + 14 = 31. Which one is the solution?
items.e: Test them: 17 + 14 = 31, so 17 is the solution. 45 + 14 = 59, 23 + 14 = 37 and 18 + 14 = 32. 45 adds 31 + 14. 23 takes the smaller digit from the larger.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: > means “is greater than”. 15 is greater than 9, so 15 > 9 is true. The open side of the sign faces the greater number. 15 < 15 is false: 15 is equal to 15, not less.

items.q: What does n < 6 mean?
items.e: < means “is less than”. n < 6 means n is less than 6: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5. 6 itself is not less than 6, so it is not a solution.

items.q: Solve: n + 5 < 12
items.e: Think of the equation n + 5 = 12 first: n = 7. Is 7 a solution? 7 + 5 = 12, which is not less than 12. Try 6: 6 + 5 = 11, and 11 < 12 is true. So n < 7. Not n < 17: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: Solve: n + 8 > 15
items.e: Think of the equation n + 8 = 15 first: n = 7. Is 7 a solution? 7 + 8 = 15, which is not greater than 15. Try 8: 8 + 8 = 16, and 16 > 15 is true. So n > 7. Not n > 23: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: Solve: 12 + n < 20
items.e: Think of the equation 12 + n = 20 first: n = 8. Is 8 a solution? 12 + 8 = 20, which is not less than 20. Try 7: 12 + 7 = 19, and 19 < 20 is true. So n < 8. Not n < 32: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: Solve: n + 9 > 17
items.e: Think of the equation n + 9 = 17 first: n = 8. Is 8 a solution? 8 + 9 = 17, which is not greater than 17. Try 9: 9 + 9 = 18, and 18 > 17 is true. So n > 8. Not n > 26: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: Solve: n − 6 > 9
items.e: Think of the equation n − 6 = 9 first: n = 15. Is 15 a solution? 15 − 6 = 9, which is not greater than 9. Try 16: 16 − 6 = 10, and 10 > 9 is true. So n > 15. Not n > 3: that subtracts instead of adding.

items.q: Solve: n − 3 > 10
items.e: Think of the equation n − 3 = 10 first: n = 13. Is 13 a solution? 13 − 3 = 10, which is not greater than 10. Try 14: 14 − 3 = 11, and 11 > 10 is true. So n > 13. Not n > 7: that subtracts instead of adding.

items.q: The dots show all the whole-number solutions. Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The dots are on 0 to 5, so the graph shows n < 6. Solve n + 4 < 10: think n + 4 = 10, so n = 6, and n + 4 < 10 gives n < 6.

items.q: The dots show all the whole-number solutions. Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The dots are on 9, 10, 11 and so on, so the graph shows n > 8. Solve n + 7 > 15: think n + 7 = 15, so n = 8, and n + 7 > 15 gives n > 8.

items.q: The dots show all the whole-number solutions. Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The dots are on 0 to 2, so the graph shows n < 3. Solve n + 9 < 12: think n + 9 = 12, so n = 3, and n + 9 < 12 gives n < 3.

items.q: The dots show all the whole-number solutions. Which inequality does the graph show?
items.e: The dots are on 13, 14, 15 and so on, so the graph shows n > 12. Solve n − 4 > 8: think n − 4 = 8, so n = 12, and n − 4 > 8 gives n > 12.

items.q: How do you graph the whole-number solutions of n + 3 < 9?
items.e: Solve first: n + 3 < 9 gives n < 6. The whole numbers less than 6 are 0 to 5, so put dots on 0 to 5. 6 is not less than 6, so it gets no dot.

items.q: How do you graph the whole-number solutions of n + 6 > 14?
items.e: Solve first: n + 6 > 14 gives n > 8. Put dots on 9 and greater and an arrow to show they keep going. 8 itself is not greater than 8, so it gets no dot.

items.q: How do you graph the whole-number solutions of n − 5 > 6?
items.e: Solve first: n − 5 > 6 gives n > 11. Put dots on 12 and greater and an arrow to show they keep going. 11 itself is not greater than 11, so it gets no dot. Not 2 and greater: that subtracts 5 instead of adding it.

items.q: Which number is a solution of n + 6 < 15?
items.e: Test each number. Is the left side less than 15? 5 + 6 = 11 (yes); 9 + 6 = 15 (no); 10 + 6 = 16 (no); 12 + 6 = 18 (no). So the answer is 5. 9 + 6 = 15 is equal to 15, not less, so 9 is not a solution.

items.q: Which number is a solution of n + 4 > 11?
items.e: Test each number. Is the left side greater than 11? 9 + 4 = 13 (yes); 7 + 4 = 11 (no); 6 + 4 = 10 (no); 3 + 4 = 7 (no). So the answer is 9.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of n − 2 > 10?
items.e: Test each number. Is the left side greater than 10? 12 − 2 = 10 (no); 13 − 2 = 11 (yes); 15 − 2 = 13 (yes); 18 − 2 = 16 (yes). So the answer is 12. 12 − 2 = 10 is equal to 10, not greater, so 12 is not a solution.

items.q: Olivia graphs the whole-number solutions of n + 2 > 9 like this. What is wrong?
c: The dots should be on 0 to 7
The dots should be on 7 and greater
The dots should be on 8 and greater
items.e: n + 2 > 9 gives n > 7: the numbers greater than 7. So the dots go on 8 and greater, with an arrow. Olivia mixed up > and < and put dots on the wrong side. 7 gets no dot: 7 + 2 = 9 is not greater than 9.

items.q: Mei graphs the whole-number solutions of n + 5 < 11 like this. What is wrong?
c: The dots should be on 7 and greater
items.e: n + 5 < 11 gives n < 6. 6 + 5 = 11, which is not less than 11, so 6 should not have a dot. 0 is a solution: 0 + 5 = 5, and 5 < 11.

sets.title: Word problems with equations and inequalities

items.q: Leah has 18 hockey cards. She gets n more cards. Now she has 35. Which equation shows this?
items.e: Leah starts with 18, gets n more and ends with 35: 18 + n = 35. Then n = 35 − 18 = 17.

items.q: Amira picks 14 apples at the orchard. Her brother picks some too. Together they have 32 apples. How many apples did her brother pick?
items.e: Equation: 14 + n = 32. n = 32 − 14 = 18 apples. Check: 14 + 18 = 32. Not 46: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 22: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: A teacher puts 24 chairs in 4 equal rows for an assembly. Let n be the number of chairs in each row. Which equation matches?
items.e: 4 rows with n chairs in each is 4 × n, and that is 24 chairs: 4 × n = 24. Then n = 6.

items.q: Hot chocolate at the skating rink costs $3 a cup. Hana buys some cups for her friends and pays $27. How many cups did she buy?
items.e: Equation: 3 × n = 27. n = 27 ÷ 3 = 9 cups. Check: 3 × 9 = 27. Not 24: that subtracts 3. Not 81: that multiplies.

items.q: Each canoe holds 2 campers. There are 34 campers on the canoe trip. How many canoes do they need?
items.e: Equation: 2 × n = 34. n = 34 ÷ 2 = 17 canoes. Check: 2 × 17 = 34. Not 68: that multiplies. Not 32: that subtracts 2.

items.q: A Grade 4 class has raised $28 for the Terry Fox Run. The goal is $50. How much more do they need to raise?
items.e: Equation: 28 + n = 50. n = 50 − 28 = $22. Check: $28 + $22 = $50. Not $78: that adds instead of subtracting. Not $38: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: There were some Canada geese on a pond. 17 flew away, and 26 are left. How many geese were there at the start?
items.e: Equation: n − 17 = 26. Undo − 17 by adding: n = 26 + 17 = 43 geese. Check: 43 − 17 = 26. Not 9: that subtracts instead of adding. Not 33: that forgets to carry the ten.

items.q: Ava had n stickers. She gave 12 to friends and has 19 left. Which equation matches?
items.e: Start with n, give away 12, and 19 are left: n − 12 = 19. Then n = 19 + 12 = 31.

items.q: Kai shares some maple candies equally among 6 friends. Each friend gets 7 candies. How many candies did he share?
items.e: Equation: n ÷ 6 = 7. Multiplication undoes division: n = 7 × 6 = 42 candies. Check: 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Not 13: that adds. Not 36 or 48: that gives each friend 6 or 8 candies instead of 7.

items.q: A school bus holds 48 students. 29 students are on the bus. How many more students can get on?
items.e: Equation: 29 + n = 48. n = 48 − 29 = 19 students. Check: 29 + 19 = 48. Not 77: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 21: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: For Thanksgiving, Grandma cuts each pie into 8 equal pieces. There are 40 pieces. How many pies are there?
items.e: Equation: 8 × n = 40. n = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 pies. Check: 8 × 5 = 40. Not 32: that subtracts 8. Not 320: that multiplies.

items.q: A ringette team has 12 players. The coach can add n more players, but the team must have fewer than 18 players. Which inequality matches?
items.e: 12 players plus n more must be fewer than 18, so use <: 12 + n < 18. Not =: the team does not have to have exactly 18.

items.q: A ringette team has 12 players. The team must have fewer than 18 players, so 12 + n < 18. What is the greatest number of players the coach can add?
items.e: 12 + n < 18 gives n < 6. The greatest whole number less than 6 is 5. Check: 12 + 5 = 17 and 17 < 18. Not 6: 12 + 6 = 18, which is not fewer than 18. Not 30: that adds.

items.q: Owen has read 9 books. To win a prize, he must read more than 14 books in all, so 9 + n > 14. What is the fewest more books he can read to win?
items.e: 9 + n > 14 gives n > 5. The least whole number greater than 5 is 6. Check: 9 + 6 = 15 and 15 > 14. Not 5: 9 + 5 = 14, which is not more than 14. Not 23: that adds.

items.q: Priya has $35. She buys a hockey stick and has $12 left. How much did the stick cost?
items.e: Equation: 35 − n = 12. n = 35 − 12 = $23. Check: $35 − $23 = $12. Not $47: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: 32 students go on a field trip in 4 vans. Each van has the same number of students. How many students are in each van?
items.e: Equation: 4 × n = 32. n = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 students. Check: 4 × 8 = 32. Not 28: that subtracts 4. Not 128: that multiplies.

items.q: Chloe puts the same number of photos, n, on each of 5 pages of her scrapbook. She uses 30 photos. Which equation matches?
items.e: 5 pages with n photos on each is 5 × n: 5 × n = 30. Then n = 30 ÷ 5 = 6.

items.q: In a board game, Aiden has 11 points. He wins with more than 20 points. Which number of extra points lets him win?
items.e: 11 + n > 20 gives n > 9. Test 10: 11 + 10 = 21, and 21 > 20, so 10 works. 9 does not: 11 + 9 = 20 is equal to 20, not more than 20.

items.q: Liam has 15 red blocks and 20 blue blocks. Ethan has 25 red blocks. How many blue blocks does Ethan need to have the same number of blocks as Liam?
items.e: Equation: 15 + 20 = 25 + n. 15 + 20 = 35. So 25 + n = 35, and n = 10 blue blocks. Not 35: that is Liam’s total. Not 30: 25 is more than 15, so Ethan needs fewer than 20 blue blocks, not more.

items.q: Nathan’s family drives 50 km to the cottage. They stop after 18 km, then drive 14 km more and stop again. How far do they still have to drive?
items.e: Equation: 18 + 14 + n = 50. 18 + 14 = 32. So 32 + n = 50, and n = 50 − 32 = 18 km. Not 32: that forgets the 14 km. Not 36: that forgets the first 18 km. Not 82: that adds all the numbers.
